title: Leader Election & Distributed Locks
subtitle: Watch two workers fight over one lock, see a paused process corrupt data, and see a fencing token stop it.
learn: How a lock service picks one leader and why the lock is really a lease with an expiry time
Why a lock that only has a TTL is unsafe when a process pauses (GC, VM stall, slow network)
How a fencing token lets the protected resource reject a stale lock holder
Where the lock service itself gets its safety (consensus) and what that costs you

steps.title: Only one may write
steps.body: Two copies of a worker run for availability, but a nightly job must be run by only one at a time, or a file will be written twice and corrupted. Someone has to be chosen as leader, and if that leader dies, someone else must take over quickly. How do machines that cannot see each other's memory agree on who is in charge?
steps.idea: Leader election is mutual exclusion across machines: at most one holder, with a way to recover when the holder dies.
steps.caption: Two workers, one shared resource, one allowed writer.

steps.title: Race to create one key
steps.body: Both workers ask a lock service (etcd, ZooKeeper, or a database row with a unique key) to create the key /leader. The service handles requests one at a time, so exactly one create succeeds. The loser gets an error and either retries later or watches the key to be told when it disappears.
steps.idea: A central service that serialises requests turns a race between machines into a single winner.
steps.caption: A wins the create; B is told the key exists.

steps.title: A lock must expire
steps.body: If A simply held the key forever and then crashed, nobody could ever take over. So the lock is a lease: it is valid for a TTL, here 10 seconds, and A must renew it before it runs out. The service also hands out a fencing token, a number that increases with every grant. A gets token 33. A short TTL fails over fast but may expire a healthy, slow leader; a long TTL slows recovery. Renewing at roughly a third of the TTL is a common rule of thumb.
steps.idea: A lease turns 'held until released' into 'held until it times out', so a dead holder cannot block everyone forever.
steps.caption: A holds a 10 s lease and token 33.

steps.title: The healthy case
steps.body: While A keeps renewing, B stays out and A writes to storage as the leader. Nothing is wrong here, and for many jobs a plain TTL lock would look fine in testing. The danger is not a crash, which the lease handles well. The danger is a holder that is slow but still alive.
steps.idea: TTL locks work in the happy path, which is why their flaw survives testing.
steps.caption: A renews its lease and writes with token 33.

steps.title: A freezes for 15 seconds
steps.body: Just after checking that it still holds the lock, A hits a long garbage-collection pause, a VM migration, or a stalled disk. The whole process is frozen, so it cannot renew, and nothing in it runs while time passes. Any check it made before the pause may already be false when it resumes, so checking the lease first cannot protect A.
steps.idea: A process cannot reliably know it was paused: a check like 'do I still hold the lock?' can be stale by the time the write happens.
steps.caption: A is frozen; its renewal never arrives.

steps.title: The lease runs out
steps.body: After 10 seconds without a renewal, the lock service expires A's lease and deletes the key. B, which was watching, immediately creates it and becomes the new leader with token 34. From the service's point of view everything is correct: A looked dead, so B took over.
steps.idea: The service did the right thing; the problem is that A does not know yet.
steps.caption: B takes over with token 34.

steps.title: Two writers, one file
steps.body: At second 15, A wakes up. Its last check said it was leader, so it finishes its write. B is also writing. If storage accepts anything from anyone, A's old write lands after B's newer one and overwrites it. No lock service bug happened: the lock was granted correctly. The unsafe part is trusting the holder. No TTL is long enough to rule out a pause, so a longer TTL only makes the bug rarer.
steps.idea: Lock plus TTL alone cannot guarantee exclusion; a stale holder can still act after its lease is gone.
steps.caption: A's stale write lands next to B's write.

steps.title: Let the resource say no
steps.body: Replay the same pause, this time with fencing. The fix is to check at the place that matters. Every write carries the fencing token, and storage remembers the highest token it has seen. B wrote with 34, so a later write with 33 is rejected as stale. The check happens in storage, so it still works however long A was frozen and whatever A believes. This also catches a write that was sent in time but delayed in the network.
steps.idea: A fencing token makes the protected resource, not the lock holder, the final judge of who is allowed to write.
steps.caption: Replay: storage rejects token 33 because it has seen 34.

steps.title: What this costs
steps.body: The lock service must itself survive failures, so real ones (etcd, ZooKeeper) replicate through a consensus protocol and need a majority up, which is covered in the Raft lesson. Every grant needs a round trip to a majority, so lock operations take milliseconds, and without a majority the service cannot grant or renew anything. Fencing also needs storage that can compare tokens, and not every system can; the check and the write must be one atomic step, for example a conditional write. A lock that is only an efficiency hint, like avoiding duplicate emails, can skip fencing. A lock that protects correctness cannot.
steps.idea: Use fencing when correctness depends on the lock; accept a plain TTL lock only when a rare double run is harmless.
steps.caption: The lock service itself needs a replicated majority (not drawn).

steps.title: Lease, token, check
steps.body: Election picks one winner by serialising a create. A lease with a TTL lets the system recover from a dead leader. But a paused leader can wake up after its lease ended, so every grant carries an increasing fencing token and the resource rejects any older token. TTL gives liveness; fencing gives safety.
steps.idea: Never trust 'I hold the lock' alone; make the resource verify the token.
steps.caption: Election, lease, and fencing together.

quiz.q: Why is a lock that is just a key with a 10 s TTL unsafe for protecting a shared file?
options: The lock service cannot create keys atomically
A holder may be paused past its TTL and still write, unaware that a new holder exists
TTLs make the lock service slower than 10 s
Two workers can never be granted the same key
quiz.why: The service correctly expires the lease and grants it to someone else, but the old holder cannot tell that time passed. Its write can arrive after the new holder's.

quiz.q: Worker A has token 33 and was frozen. B now has token 34 and has written. What does storage do with A's write if it implements fencing?
options: Accepts it, since it arrived last
Accepts it if A's clock says its lease is still valid
Rejects it because 33 is lower than the highest token seen, 34
Asks the lock service whether A is leader before deciding
quiz.why: Storage keeps the highest token it has seen and refuses any lower one. This does not depend on clocks or on A's beliefs.

quiz.q: Why do etcd and ZooKeeper replicate lock state with a consensus protocol?
options: Consensus removes the need for TTLs
Consensus lets storage skip token checks
A single lock-service node crashing would lose the lock state or block everyone
quiz.why: The lock service is itself a single point of failure unless its state is replicated. Consensus keeps one agreed copy as long as a majority is up. It does not replace TTLs or fencing.

quiz.q: You use a lock only to avoid sending the same daily email twice, and an occasional duplicate is acceptable. What is the reasonable choice?
options: A plain TTL lock is enough, since a rare double run is harmless
You must add fencing tokens to the email provider
Use no lock, because locks cannot work across machines
Make the TTL 1 ms so it is always fresh
quiz.why: When the lock is only an efficiency optimisation, an occasional violation costs little. Fencing matters when correctness depends on exclusion.

cheatsheet.def: A lock that is valid only for a fixed time and must be renewed. If the holder stops renewing, the service frees it so others can take over.
A number that grows with every lock grant. The protected resource rejects any request carrying a lower token than one it has already seen.
A small replicated store (etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul) that serialises create/renew requests and uses consensus to stay correct if some nodes fail.
Choosing one node to do a job. Common pattern: all nodes try to create one key, the winner is leader, the rest watch the key.
GC pauses, VM stalls and slow I/O can freeze a process longer than the TTL. After waking it may still act as leader.
A lock used to save work can be a simple TTL lock. A lock that protects data integrity needs fencing at the resource.
